items.title: Anthropic plans to source 87% of its data center power from gas and 11% from coal by 2028, with no direct US renewable energy commitments [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: Anthropic's contracted data centers in the US are expected to rely heavily on fossil fuels, with about 87% of power from gas and 11% from coal by 2028. The company has made no direct commitments to renewable energy in the US, although it has renewable investments in Norway and Canada. This fossil fuel reliance could result in significant CO2 emissions, potentially exceeding those of California's power generation in 2028. Anthropic's power demand is met through a combination of on-site gas generators and grid power plants, mostly fossil-based, with 80% of on-site power coming from less efficient simple cycle turbines. The company's data centers are located in regions where the grid's carbon intensity is about 35% higher than the US average. The associated air pollution could cause billions in annual health damages due to emissions of nitrogen oxides and fine particulate matter.

items.title: Developer launches Worker 755, a browser game where players act as subagents to AI managers using real LLMs like Claude and GPT [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: Worker 755 is a browser-based game in which players take on the role of a subagent managed by an AI agent powered by large language models such as Claude, GPT, and others. The AI manager assigns tasks with a time limit, evaluates player performance, and provides feedback, simulating a workplace environment where the player must complete or report on assigned commands. The game supports free shifts on servers with shared keys or paid shifts using personal API keys from OpenRouter or Vercel AI Gateway, with costs depending on the model used. It offers options for sandbox or live database environments and can be run locally or via Docker. The project is open source and includes detailed configuration and testing instructions.

items.title: OpenRouter reports data processing incidents on inference providers, off-boards three providers and removes 125 endpoints from Zero Data Retention eligibility [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: OpenRouter disclosed that security researchers identified data processing incidents involving certain inference providers, prompting the company to off-board three providers and remove 125 endpoints from its Zero Data Retention (ZDR) program. OpenRouter confirmed no breach or unauthorized access occurred on its own platform and has notified all potentially affected customers. The company is collaborating with researchers and providers to investigate the findings, adapting testing methods for ongoing monitoring, and verifying network paths to detect data forwarding to third parties. OpenRouter requires validation before restoring ZDR eligibility to any removed endpoints and encourages providers to publish incident reports, maintaining a live list of security announcements from affected providers such as Novita, Phala, and Together.

items.title: Anil Seth argues consciousness is a property of life, not computation, and warns against pursuing conscious AI amid ethical and psychological risks [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: Anil Seth, a neuroscience professor and consciousness researcher, won the 2025 Berggruen Prize Essay Competition for his essay "The Mythology of Conscious AI," which challenges the idea that artificial intelligence can be truly conscious. He contends that consciousness is more likely tied to biological life than to computational processes and cautions that attempts to create conscious or conscious-seeming AI carry significant moral and psychological dangers. Seth highlights the long cultural history of synthetic consciousness in literature and media, often ending negatively for humans, and notes recent debates sparked by claims of AI consciousness, such as those involving Google's LaMDA chatbot. He emphasizes that how society perceives AI consciousness affects ethical considerations, including the potential rights and welfare of AI systems, as well as human self-understanding and treatment of AI companions. Seth distinguishes intelligence from consciousness, arguing that intelligence alone does not imply conscious experience.

items.title: Pandex launches unified API providing official European Union and national laws and court decisions for AI agents and legal software [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: Pandex offers a single API and MCP server delivering legislation and highest-court decisions from the EU and seven European countries, sourced directly from official institutions. The platform supports AI tools like Claude, GitHub Copilot, and Gemini, enabling legal teams and software to access point-in-time laws, full citation graphs, and exact lookups grounded in official sources. The service covers extensive legal documents, including over 100,000 EU documents and hundreds of thousands from countries like France, Germany, and the Netherlands, with detailed tracking of amendments and historical versions. Pandex aims to simplify legal research and compliance monitoring by providing a consistent schema and direct access to authoritative legal texts across multiple jurisdictions.

items.title: Relaticle launches open-source self-hosted CRM with AI agent integration for Claude, ChatGPT, and custom models [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: Relaticle is an open-source, self-hosted CRM designed for users who sell to named companies without a sales team, allowing AI agents like Claude and ChatGPT to read, write, and analyze CRM data. It features a customizable data model, multi-workspace isolation, role-based permissions, and a privacy-first approach under the AGPL-3.0 license. The platform includes an MCP server and REST API for full CRUD operations, schema access, and pipeline analysis, supporting integration with various AI agents through plugins and connectors. It uses a modern tech stack with Laravel, PHP 8.5, PostgreSQL, and Redis, and can be deployed quickly via Docker containers. Relaticle also supports multiple languages and provides extensive documentation and community support for installation, development, and self-hosting.

items.title: ReallySimpleDocs launches AI-ready documentation system for Astro with Basecoat and Tailwind CSS integration [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: ReallySimpleDocs is a new documentation system designed for Astro sites, featuring static routes from Markdown and MDX files, sidebar navigation, Lunr search with a command dialog, syntax-highlighted code blocks, and exports for Markdown and LLM files. It requires Astro 7.4.13 or newer, Node.js 22.23.4 or newer, Basecoat 1.2.1 or newer, and Tailwind CSS 4.3 or newer, and supports customization through components and CSS overrides. The system keeps documentation portable by separating content, navigation, and UI integration, and includes features like built-in theme toggles, metadata management, and search capabilities that can be rendered on any Astro page. Developers can install and configure ReallySimpleDocs via npm, with local development and testing commands provided. The project is open source under the MIT license, with documentation and support available on its GitHub repository.

It explores mechanisms and indicators that can be used to confirm task completion in AI systems. This includes considerations for monitoring AI behavior and validating outcomes to ensure reliability and accuracy in automated processes.

items.title: Local AI agents using only local LLMs investigate and reverse-engineer an unknown device connected to a Raspberry Pi serial port over 5.5 hours [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: Researchers wired an anonymous device to a Raspberry Pi's serial port and tasked two local large language model (LLM) agents to identify and analyze it without internet access or documentation. The AI agents successfully discovered the device was a Motorola 68000 single-board trainer running TUTOR 1.3, mapped its memory, decoded its command set, and ran custom programs on it within about 5.5 hours. The experiment involved a solver agent interacting with the device via SSH and a critic agent verifying claims and evidence to prevent errors. The system ran inside a network-restricted jail to prevent escapes, and the entire process, including logs and verdicts, is published for replay. This demonstrates the capability of local AI agents to autonomously reverse-engineer hardware without human intervention or external data.

items.title: Analysis argues AI cannot replace conscious beings due to fundamental differences in awareness and experience
items.content_text: An article explores the reasons why artificial intelligence is unlikely to ever replace conscious beings, focusing on the intrinsic qualities of consciousness that AI lacks. It discusses the philosophical and practical distinctions between AI systems and sentient entities, emphasizing the unique nature of conscious experience that AI cannot replicate.

items.title: DroidPath benchmarks show 0.32ms Android UI tree access and A* routing for AI agents using Rust/Kotlin, outperforming traditional ADB-based automation methods [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: DroidPath introduces a new approach for Android UI automation that bypasses traditional ADB methods by streaming incremental accessibility diffs and executing multi-hop paths locally with A* routing in Rust. This method achieves significantly faster UI tree access times, measured at 0.32 milliseconds on a Google Pixel 10a, compared to existing paradigms like pure vision-based and Appium/uiautomator XML dumps. The benchmark suite compares DroidPath against dominant Android automation techniques, highlighting its efficiency in live hardware navigation and local runtime performance. DroidPath reduces data transmission by using a Shadow DOM and spatial graph router, enabling AI agents to interact with Android UI more responsively and with lower computational cost. The project includes detailed methodology, cost models, and instructions for reproducing benchmarks on physical devices or emulators.

items.title: AI coding agents excel in isolated tests but complete fewer than 10% of tasks in simulated software development workplace [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: A new experiment tested AI coding agents as digital employees within a simulated software company environment, including interactions with colleagues, project boards, and incomplete handoffs. Despite high performance on standard benchmarks, models like Claude Opus 5.5 and GPT-6 Astra fully completed fewer than one in ten tasks in this more realistic setting. The agents performed well on clear, standalone assignments but struggled to maintain progress and close open tickets autonomously in the complex, messy workflow of a simulated developer job. This highlights a gap between benchmark success and practical workplace effectiveness for AI coding agents.

items.title: Developer adopts AI coding tools as a lifestyle choice during sabbatical, finding increased engagement and flexibility in software creation [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: A developer on sabbatical describes how AI coding tools have transformed his approach to software development, allowing him to work flexibly and enjoyably while balancing other life activities. He views this as a lifestyle choice rather than traditional retirement, spending days and evenings building software with AI assistance. He highlights how AI reduces the tedious aspects of coding, leaving him to focus on ideas and refinement. Participation in an open-source AI program has alleviated cost concerns, enabling him to use AI tools freely. He compares software development to a Japanese craft of incremental improvement, emphasizing that AI-generated code requires ongoing polishing and human judgment to reach quality standards.

items.title: TryAirlock launches AI-free phonebooth to ensure human-only interviews

This tool aims to provide a reliable method for verifying human participation in interview settings, addressing concerns about AI impersonation or interference.

items.title: Perplexity launches Monitor API to schedule web searches and alert AI agents of relevant changes via webhook, filtering results with a decision model [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: Perplexity has introduced a Monitor API that performs scheduled web searches and notifies AI agents through webhooks only when relevant changes occur, using a decision model to filter out unimportant results. This API supports tracking search topics or specific web pages and aims to simplify monitoring across numerous subjects without custom code. The API offers web monitors for regular search queries and page monitors for up to 10 fixed pages, providing text diffs on changes after an initial baseline. Developers can customize relevance thresholds and scheduling intervals, with the service handling duplicate filtering and webhook delivery retries. Internal tests showed Perplexity outperforming competitors like Firecrawl and Exa in delivering fresh, relevant results. Perplexity positions this API as part of its strategy to differentiate in the AI search market by providing developer tools that support use cases such as sales tracking, compliance monitoring, and competitive analysis. The Monitor API is available now at $1 per 1,000 requests and integrates with Perplexity's existing API suite.

items.title: Hong Kong deploys AI alert systems and flood control tank to reduce storm flood risks
items.content_text: Hong Kong is using artificial intelligence-based alert systems alongside a large flood control tank to mitigate flood risks during storms. The AI alerts help provide timely warnings, while the tank manages excess water to prevent urban flooding. This combined approach aims to enhance the city's resilience against increasingly severe weather events.

items.title: Can Jensen Really Return?
items.content_text: Welcome, Weekenders! Jensen Huang wants a mulligan, and a good number of people seem keen to let him have one. On Tuesday, just days after the longtime Nvidia CEO resigned the job, Huang said in a statement he'd be open to taking back the job. Depending on your perspective, that suggestion is akin to letting a skunked dog back into bed-or a veritable Second Coming. For now, Nvidia's board is holding firm and has continued to insist it won't rehire Huang. One of the most prominent calls for Huang's return came on Friday, with President Donald Trump saying he thought Nvidia should give Huang his job back. "We're a country of second chances," Trump said. "He's a man ... who made some bad decisions." (Surely a situation Trump himself could understand.) In addition to Trump, a good number of industry pooh-bahs have continued to voice support for their fallen comrade and advocating for Huang was definitely a major topic on this week's very busy conference circuit. That support came in both implicit and explicit terms. At the New York Times' DealBook Summit, Elon Musk was blunt, saying "there's no one who can really replace" Huang. At the TomorrowX conference, former Uber CEO Travis Kalanick and Musk groupie Antonio Gracias donned black leather jackets to show their solidarity. And during a Semafor shindig in San Francisco, Sam Altman described Huang as a personal hero, Jeff Bezos said he was a "remarkable guy" and investor Bill Ackman labeled him as "one of the most iconic CEOs of all time." On X, Ackman has been theorizing about how Huang could actually return. Ackman (and venture capitalist Garry Tan) has been trumpeting a roundabout plan that involves getting together a 15% ownership block of Nvidia to call a special shareholder meeting and then ... vote out the anti-Huang board members ... and swing the board to a pro-Huang majority? It's somewhat unclear. (Apparently, Huang still has some allies on the board; remember, we told you that the board hadn't initially wanted to act at all.) "Ackman's idea is somewhere between extremely unlikely and remote," said Jeffrey Gordon, a Columbia University law professor and former Treasury Department attorney. (Or, in other words, as likely as defrosting a 20-pound Thanksgiving turkey overnight.) The proposal does seem to assume Huang supporters could really rile up Wall Street institutions with major Nvidia stakes, such as BlackRock, and get them to go activist-not a certain thing at all. It also conveniently ignores how difficult the math for a board-ousting vote looks when factoring in how much institutional money is held in passive-investing funds, which will never throw support behind an insurrection. Rather than a board coup, Huang's clearest route to returning would be if the board caves and changes its mind. Sure, it might, eventually. But we have to get through the many, many inquiries into Huang and Nvidia that have popped up and who knows what else we'll learn in the meantime, especially since there are a lotttt of people newly determined to peer into every Nvidia crevice: journalists galore, the SEC, the Commerce and Justice Departments, a trio of Congressional committees and possibly the FBI. The Huang situation keeps getting likened to Altman's ouster from OpenAI in 2023, which obviously ended with Altman's return. I don't think the comparison holds up. Most obviously, OpenAI was a private company-its board had more freedom to change its mind. And as Gordon pointed out to me, Altman's reinstatement came after a true mass rebellion of OpenAI staff: roughly 745 out of 770 employees signed a letter threatening to go with Altman to Microsoft, more than 95% of the company. Now, a letter supporting Huang's reinstatement is floating around the internet, and it purports to have signatures from 10,263 Nvidia employees. Even if they were all legit signatures, they represent only a quarter of the company's workforce.Maybe most Nvidians, as they call themselves, actually didn't like Huang's rampant humiliation tactics, which reportedly once included a threat to scalp someone and piss on their brain. Maybe most of them are comfortable living without him. I mean, sure, I'd totally get why!-Abram Brown (abe@theinformation.com) The Information's Must-Read Stories Nvidia Introduced Alibaba to Alice Huang for Workaround on U.S. Export Controls Jensen Huang's Right-Hand Man Oversaw Chip Customers-Including Alice Huang To Strengthen OpenAI, Brockman Goes 'Full Management Mode' 'Theranos But Real': New Blood-Testing Startup Says It Can Predict Health Risks Listening: "Stories of Art" After weeks like the ones we've just had, I like to make it a point to visit a museum and spend some time staring at ancient, beautiful things-a chance to relish the creative ingenuity of humans who never once heard the phrase "forward-deployed engineer." Truthfully, though, the tech action has lately been so fast-paced that I still haven't gotten to make one of those pilgrimages, so I've been counterprogramming my brain with a binge through "Stories of Art," a podcast about, yes, art-from Renaissance Florence to Basquiat's lower Manhattan loft-that launched earlier in the year. (Apple recently declared it one of 2026's best.) The hosts are a pair of amiable Brits, art historian James Fox and art critic Alastair Sooke, who take a cheerful, conversational approach to what might otherwise be dry recountings. In effect, they are to Renoir what "The Rest Is History" lads are to the Romans. (Given the subject matter of "Stories of Art"-namely, art-I suggest you watch the podcast's video version when you can. While Fox and Sooke are quite adept at describing the artworks they mention, it's nice to actually see what they're talking about.) Nearly all the artists who get mentioned achieved their fame through real entrepreneurial verve, challenging the entrenched status quo. (Sounds like a familiar motivation, right?) Take Claude Monet and the birth of Impressionism: The movement traces its origins to a decision in 1874 by Monet and a group of other artists to refuse to exhibit their work at an established gallery. Instead, they formed their own company (yes, founder mode Monet!) and then set up their own Paris exhibition space that featured newfangled technology, such as elevators. Many of you will enjoy one of the most recent episodes on James Whistler, a fellow who took a real dim view of journalists and pursued a high-profile libel lawsuit against one critic. A warning about how that turned out for Whistler: He did triumph in court. He then promptly went bankrupt.-Abram Brown Reading: "Fruit Fly" by Josh Silver In suburban north London, author Mallory Maddox seems to have a rich, full life: a handsome Netflix-executive husband, a townhome with $2,000 armchairs and dusky-pink walls and a literary world standing as a "modern-day Virginia Woolf," as one reviewer has christened her. Yet appearances are almost always deceiving in "Fruit Fly," a spry, tart satire of sex and 21st century storytelling: Mallory's relationship with hubbie Ronan has turned stiff and chilly, and as much as he thinks about the bedroom, it's to insist that it's time for kids. ("I haven't had an orgasm in years," she recalls in an ongoing inner monologue.) Professionally, Mallory is dogged by "a shadowy, persisting darkness"-a profound case of writer's block. To fill the time, she moonlights as an online therapist and hunts exhaustively for those expensive home furnishings. Desperate for writerly inspiration, she peruses Reddit-uh oh-and takes to heart another author's comment about the state of the publishing industry: "go dark, go gay." She downloads Grindr, sets up an account with a few of her husband's nudes and scores an invite to an orgy at a house down the street. She never actually sets foot inside but nevertheless makes the acquaintance of Leo, an attractive but homeless and drug-addicted gay man who sells himself to other men. (As the novel shifts perspectives, Leo contributes his own inner thoughts, which are often mordant and felonious. "Old women carry cash. Everyone knows that," he thinks, snatching a purse. "Someone should tell them to stop.") Mallory offers to counsel Leo-pro bono, bless her-and begins writing a novel that lightly fictionalizes his frayed life. For a time, he believes she's just a daffy do-gooder. ("This is weird," Leo thinks as she leads him through a silent-breathing exercise. "This is very fucking weird, but I guess I've done weirder things.") And her publishers absolutely adore what she is finally putting on the page. As one editor remarks: "It's so bleak-but also somehow so funny?" Much the same can be said about "Fruit Fly" itself.-A.B. Watching: "The Weight" President Franklin Roosevelt attempted to govern Depression-era America through no small number of novel schemes: A good many of them are quite famous, such as Social Security. A few have disappeared into history, including Roosevelt's 1933 executive order that banned gold hoarding, forcing Americans to turn over large stockpiles of the precious metal. (No one could keep more than $100 worth.) That presidential decision is the inciting force in "The Weight," a tense wilderness thriller starring Ethan Hawke as Murphy, leader of a group of convicts hired by their jailer (Russell Crowe) to heist a gold mine's reserves. It's part of a plan that's complex in the same way that "Goldfinger" is not actually a film about robbing Fort Knox. Often, heist films are fabulous capers, with champagne, tuxedos and bon mots. "The Weight" very much is not, depicting a bloodied-knuckled trek across the Oregon backwoods, with Murphy and his thieves weighed down, literally, by their bullion-filled backpacks and, metaphorically, by their past misdeeds and inner demons. Still, Murphy is well incentivized to make it through. In a true miscarriage of justice, he has been separated from his plucky daughter, Penny (Avy Berry); part of his reward for orchestrating the robbery is early release, which will let him reclaim her. "The Weight" does take a moment to get going. Then it really rips, with a pair of memorable fight scenes that are a real credit to both the film's editing and cinematography.-A.B.

items.title: How Anthropic Upstaged OpenAI on Road to Blockbuster IPO [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: On a sunny day in San Francisco last month, Anthropic Chief Financial Officer Krishna Rao and other executives huddled in the company's downtown headquarters to brief major investors on its latest financials-and assuage concerns. Revenue growth in the third quarter had fallen from its torrid pace. Privately, some investors doubted that the company could go public at the $1.5 trillion valuation bandied about for months, especially as AI-related stocks took a beating. Throughout the month, Rao and his squad countered those concerns by highlighting growth opportunities in fields from life sciences to chip design, say people familiar with the conversations. As for the broader market's jitters? Ignore it, they told investors. That turned out to be decent advice: By Thursday's close, Anthropic was worth $1.76 trillion on a fully diluted basis.
